title: Printable abacus — Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)
header: Printable abacus — Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)

text.text:
Why this printable abacus?

The Soroban (算盤) and the Suanpan (算盤) write numbers with beads on rods: each upper bead is worth five and each lower bead is worth one. This print-and-play version follows the same board used in the online game Writing integers with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤) (), but removes the instructions panel so the printed page is only the abacus. It adapts the cut-and-play idea of Counting with the bone to a bead board ().

source.page: Writing integers with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)
Counting with the bone — Print and Play

text.text:
What you need

  • A4 paper and a printer.
  • Scissors.
  • Optional: a pencil, a glue stick or tape.

Print the six sheets that follow on A4 paper in landscape orientation. Keep the abacus sheet whole. Cut out the circles and the cards along the dashed borders.

The Suanpan board

Nine rods, two upper positions and five lower positions on each rod. Place the cut-out circles on the dashed positions to write a number.

The Soroban board

Nine rods, one upper position and four lower positions on each rod. Place the cut-out circles on the dashed positions to write a number.

Beads and decimal marker to cut

Cut out the circles along the dashed borders. Red circles are worth five, blue circles are worth one, and the black circle marks the units column.

18 red circles — each worth 5
45 blue circles — each worth 1
1 black circle — units / decimal marker

Cut along the dashed lines.

How to write a number

The cut-out circles are the discs of the abacus. Move them with your fingers exactly as you tap and slide the beads in the online game Writing numbers with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤).

  • Each of the nine rods has discs worth five above the bar (red) and discs worth one below the bar (blue).
  • A disc counts only while it touches the central bar: push a red disc down to the bar or a blue disc up to the bar; slide it back to its starting position to remove it.
  • The value of a rod is the sum of the discs touching the bar and must stay between zero and nine, so one red and four blue discs is the largest valid digit. The Suanpan uses two red and five blue discs per rod; the Soroban uses only one red and four blue discs per rod, so leave the extra discs aside.
  • A rod with no disc touching the bar is worth zero and stays empty.

Units and the decimal marker

  • Place the black disc on the bar and slide it along the bar to choose the units column, just as the decimal point (⚫) is dragged in the game.
  • The rod under the black disc is the units; the rods to its left are tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands, millions, ten millions and hundred millions — nine rods in all.
  • With the black disc on the rightmost rod you write whole numbers of up to nine digits; each place you move it to the left opens a decimal column on its right.

Examples

  1. Card 100000000 (deck A): leave the black disc on the rightmost rod and push one blue disc to the bar in the hundred millions rod. All the other rods stay empty, so the board shows 100000000.
  2. Card 5005005 (deck B): write 5 in the millions rod, 5 in the thousands rod and 5 in the units rod — one red disc each — and leave the rods between them empty.
  3. Card 123456789 (deck B): with the black disc on the rightmost rod, write one digit after another from left to right — 1 blue disc in the hundred millions rod; 2 blue in the ten millions rod; 3 blue in the millions rod; 4 blue in the hundred thousands rod; 1 red in the ten thousands rod; 1 red and 1 blue in the thousands rod; 1 red and 2 blue in the hundreds rod; 1 red and 3 blue in the tens rod; 1 red and 4 blue in the units rod.

Read the rods from left to right to obtain the number. Start with the small cards, then use the large-number cards (powers of ten and mixed values) to write numbers with up to nine digits on the same board, changing between Soroban and Suanpan whenever you like.

How to add two numbers

Adding means moving more discs to the bar. Write the first number as in the previous section, then add the second number one digit at a time, starting with the units rod and moving to the left.

  1. Write the first number on the board.
  2. In the units rod, add the units digit of the second number: push discs to the bar until the rod shows the sum of the two digits.
  3. If the rod has free positions for the digit, stop there. For 2 + 3, add three blue discs to the two already touching the bar and then exchange the five blue discs for one red disc, so the rod shows 5.
  4. If the sum reaches ten or more, use the complement of ten: carry one disc to the rod on the left and take away from the current rod discs worth the complement. For 9 + 4, add one blue disc to the tens rod and remove six in value from the units rod, that is, one red disc and one blue disc (10 − 4 = 6); the units rod keeps 3 blue discs, so the board shows 13.
  5. If the sum is below ten but the lower positions are full and the red disc is free, use the complement of five: push one red disc to the bar and slide away the blue discs that complete five. For 4 + 3, push one red disc and slide two blue discs away (5 − 3 = 2), so the rod shows 7.
  6. Continue with the tens, hundreds and the following rods. When a rod reaches ten, always carry one disc to the rod on its left before writing the next digit, and whenever a rod would have five blue discs, exchange them for one red disc so the representation stays valid.
  7. Read the rods from left to right to obtain the result, and check it against the sum written on paper.

Examples:

  • 47 + 25 = 72: write 47 (four blue discs in the tens rod and one red plus two blue in the units rod). Add 5 in the units: the rod would pass nine, so add one blue disc to the tens rod and slide the red disc away from the units (10 − 5 = 5); the units rod now shows 2. Add 2 in the tens rod: the five blue discs are exchanged for one red disc, and two more blue discs give 7 tens. The board shows 72.
  • 123456789 + 100000000 = 223456789: the black disc stays on the rightmost rod; push one more blue disc to the bar in the hundred millions rod. All the other rods keep the same digits.

The same rules work on the Suanpan and on the Soroban. The Suanpan has two red and five blue discs per rod and the Soroban has one red and four blue discs; only the discs touching the bar count, and a rod must always stay between zero and nine. On the Suanpan, the extra discs can stay in their starting positions; when a rod reaches ten, carry one disc to the rod on the left exactly as described. Practise by drawing two cards from any deck — small values first, then the large-number cards — and adding them with the discs, choosing two cards whose sum is at most 999999999 so that the result fits on the nine rods.

Credits

This printable abacus was inspired by the online game Writing integers with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤) () and follows the print-and-play format of Counting with the bone (). The board and the number cards were prepared by the History Tracers Team.
